metadata.specialty: Inherited metabolic disorders, obstetrics and gynecology
metadata.summary: This Spanish consensus provides guidance on genetic counseling and the management of Gaucher disease before pregnancy, during pregnancy, at childbirth, and after delivery, including breastfeeding and newborn care. Its recommendations draw on GRADE evidence assessment and a structured expert consensus process that also considered patients’ values and preferences. The authors report that the available evidence is limited and of low quality.

target_population: Women with Gaucher disease who wish to become pregnant
Mothers with Gaucher disease after delivery and during breastfeeding
Newborns of mothers with Gaucher disease
Patients with Gaucher disease seeking genetic preconception counseling

conditions.name: Gaucher disease
conditions.description: An inherited metabolic disorder in which mutations affecting the enzyme glucocerebrosidase (acid β-glucosidase; EC 3.2.1.45) reduce β -glucocerebrosidase activity, leading to glucosylceramide accumulation in cells of the monocyte-macrophage system.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Pregnancy may aggravate existing disease or bring previously unrecognized manifestations to attention. Its course during pregnancy varies, chiefly according to disease severity and treatment control at conception.

subtypes.name: type 1
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The non–neuropathic form has a broad clinical range, from no symptoms to severe visceral, hematologic, coagulation and skeletal disease.

subtypes.name: GD type 3
subtypes.distinguishing_features: In patients with known lung disease, pregnancy-related concern about moderate to severe pulmonary hypertension is noted.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Inform reproductive planning for people with Gaucher disease who wish to have children.

diagnostic_workup.test: Pre-conceptional genetic study of carrier status in couples
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Inform decisions about embryos carrying one GD mutation or two GD mutations.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An embryo with two mutations would be affected by GD; the mutation type and associated risk also inform decisions.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate embryos in the specified reproductive circumstances.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During in vitro fertilization when the spouse is a GD carrier, or when donor status is unknown in Ashkenazi Jews.
May be offered when the partner is a GD carrier or, with in vitro fertilization, when the donor is unknown.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess a newborn for GD instead of using a genetic test when the father's carrier status is unknown.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After birth if the father's carrier status is unknown; repetition may be considered when clinical suspicion remains high despite a negative result.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Further evaluate a newborn for GD.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be considered if clinical suspicion remains high after a negative enzymatic dry drop test.

pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Reduced enzyme activity is part of the disorder described.

genetic_molecular.clinical_significance: Mutations in the gene encoding this enzyme cause GD; possible enzyme pseudo-deficiencies require investigation if a GD carrier is identified.

conditions.name: type 1 Gaucher disease (GD)
conditions.description: The non–neuropathic form of Gaucher disease is the principal subtype addressed in the guidance on care before, during and after pregnancy.
conditions.epidemiology: The document identifies this form as the most common lysosomal storage disorder; information on reproductive outcomes is scarce and comes mainly from case series.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Manifestations range from none to splenomegaly with possible hypersplenism, thrombocytopenia, anemia and leucopenia; hepatomegaly, abnormal coagulation, bone pain, bone crises, abnormal bone (re)modelling, osteopenia, osteonecrosis, pathological fractures and, in some cases, lung involvement may occur. During pregnancy, hepatosplenomegaly, bone crises, osteoporosis, anemia or thrombocytopenia may worsen. Bleeding can complicate pregnancy, delivery and the postpartum period, particularly with impaired platelet function. Visceromegaly and orthopedic complications may influence delivery.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify problems that may need attention before a planned pregnancy.
Assess bone status as part of the pre-pregnancy evaluation.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before a planned pregnancy, including in patients who have undergone splenectomy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An inconclusive or borderline finding for PH may lead to consideration of right heart catheterization.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide the reference assessment when cardiac ultrasound is inconclusive or borderline for PH.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After assessment of the risks and benefits of this invasive test and a decision made with the patient.
During the first trimester and the second and third trimesters.

diagnostic_workup.test: calcium, vitamin D and vitamin B12 levels
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess levels relevant to pregnancy care.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During the first trimester; calcium and vitamin D are also assessed during the second and third trimesters.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Low vitamin B12 levels detected at pregnancy diagnosis, up to week 9, prompt therapeutic dosing.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess primary hemostasis and inform pregnancy and delivery care.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During the third trimester if not previously performed during pregnancy; platelet function also informs decisions about in vitro fertilization and Aspirin.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: For the assisted-reproduction assessment, the document states that functionality tests are reliable when the platelet count is greater than 100,000 /mm3.

diagnostic_workup.test: ultrasound evaluation of liver and spleen sizes
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During the last trimester if not previously performed during pregnancy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate bone crises or worsening bone pathology.

follow_up.schedule: A GD-specific program tailored to the patient and led by an expert multidisciplinary team is required during pregnancy. The guide specifies assessments in the first trimester, the second and third trimesters, and the last trimester.
recommended_tests: First trimester: lysoGb1 and/or chitotriosidase, calcium, vitamin D and vitamin B12 levels.
Second and third trimesters: lysoGb1 and/or chitotriosidase, calcium and vitamin D levels.
Third trimester: platelet function study if not already performed during pregnancy.
Last trimester: ultrasound assessment of liver and spleen sizes if not already performed during pregnancy.

conditions.name: GD type 3
conditions.description: A Gaucher disease subtype mentioned in the assessment of pregnancy-related pulmonary risk.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Patients with known lung disease are identified among those for whom the risk associated with moderate to severe pulmonary hypertension is of particular concern.

therapies_index.name: enzyme replacement therapy (ERT)
approved_indications: Treatment of Gaucher disease.
Initiation before pregnancy in women with Gaucher disease who have mild symptoms and are not receiving treatment.
Replacement for Miglustat or Eliglustat before pregnancy.
therapies_index.administration: For women with mild symptoms starting treatment before pregnancy: 60 units/kg every two weeks. Continue without interruption or modification because of pregnancy, including during the first trimester; maintain the previous dose during breastfeeding.
monitoring: Assess for exacerbation of Gaucher disease during pregnancy, which calls for dose adjustment.

therapies_index.name: velaglucerase alfa
approved_indications: Treatment of Gaucher disease as an enzyme replacement therapy.

therapies_index.name: imiglucerase
approved_indications: Treatment of Gaucher disease as an enzyme replacement therapy.

therapies_index.name: taliglucerase alfa
approved_indications: Treatment of Gaucher disease as an enzyme replacement therapy.

therapies_index.name: substrate reduction therapy (SRT)
approved_indications: Treatment of Gaucher disease.

therapies_index.name: Miglustat
approved_indications: Treatment of Gaucher disease as a substrate reduction therapy.
therapies_index.administration: Discontinue and change to enzyme replacement therapy at least 3 months before pregnancy. Do not use during breastfeeding.

therapies_index.name: Eliglustat
approved_indications: Treatment of Gaucher disease as a substrate reduction therapy.
therapies_index.administration: Discontinue and change to enzyme replacement therapy at least 3 months before pregnancy. Do not use during breastfeeding.

therapies_index.name: bisphosphonates
therapies_index.administration: Stop at least 6 months before pregnancy; long-lasting bisphosphonates should be stopped before their intended effect ends if that requires a longer interval. Do not use during breastfeeding.

therapies_index.name: Aspirin
approved_indications: May be used during a pregnancy achieved through in vitro fertilization in a woman with Gaucher disease, subject to platelet count and normal platelet function.
monitoring: Assess platelet count and platelet function.
Assess risks associated with acetyl salicylic acid (ASA) when making a shared decision about assisted reproduction.

therapies_index.name: calcium
approved_indications: Supplementation during pregnancy and breastfeeding in women with Gaucher disease.

therapies_index.name: vitamin D
approved_indications: Supplementation during pregnancy and breastfeeding in women with Gaucher disease.
monitoring: Measure vitamin D levels during pregnancy.

therapies_index.name: vitamin B12
approved_indications: Preventive supplementation before and during pregnancy to provide the required daily dose.
Therapeutic supplementation when low levels are found at pregnancy diagnosis, up to week 9.
therapies_index.administration: Provide the required daily dose preventively before and during pregnancy; use therapeutic doses if low levels are detected at pregnancy diagnosis, up to week 9.
monitoring: Measure vitamin B12 levels during the first trimester.

therapies_index.name: vaccination against pneumococcus
approved_indications: Vaccination before a planned pregnancy in women with Gaucher disease who have undergone splenectomy.

therapies_index.name: vaccination against meningococcus
approved_indications: Vaccination before a planned pregnancy in women with Gaucher disease who have undergone splenectomy.

therapies_index.name: vaccination against Haemophilus influenzae
approved_indications: Vaccination before a planned pregnancy in women with Gaucher disease who have undergone splenectomy.

therapies_index.name: vaccination against influenza
approved_indications: Vaccination before a planned pregnancy in women with Gaucher disease who have undergone splenectomy.

therapies_index.name: COVID-19 vaccine
approved_indications: Vaccination for adults without a spleen, as cited from Centers for disease control and prevention (CDC) guidance.
therapies_index.administration: Primary series plus booster doses when eligible.

therapies_index.name: assisted reproduction techniques
approved_indications: Reproductive assistance for patients with Gaucher disease and fertility problems; compatible with enzyme replacement therapy (ERT).
key_toxicities: The risk–benefit assessment includes fetal loss and bleeding from ovarian puncture.
monitoring: Individualize the decision according to Gaucher disease status, platelet count and, when the count is greater than 100,000 /mm3, platelet function.
Assess the risks of acetyl salicylic acid (ASA) use and make a shared decision about assisted reproduction.

therapies_index.name: in vitro fertilization (IVF)
approved_indications: An assisted reproduction option for patients with Gaucher disease and fertility problems.
key_toxicities: Ovarian puncture bleeding is a risk to consider.
The procedure may pose a thrombosis risk.
monitoring: Consider platelet count and function because abnormalities may affect the procedure.

therapies_index.name: pre-implantation genetic diagnosis
approved_indications: In in vitro fertilization, offer when the partner carries Gaucher disease; the guidance also addresses an unknown donor in Ashkenazi Jews.
monitoring: When carrier status is detected, investigate possible glucocerebrosidase pseudodeficiency.
Discuss the uncertain balance of fetal loss and ovarian puncture bleeding with the patient and family, and plan to record outcomes in an active Gaucher disease pregnancy sub-registry.

therapies_index.name: prenatal genetic diagnosis
approved_indications: May be offered during pregnancy when the partner carries Gaucher disease or when the donor is unknown in a pregnancy achieved through in vitro fertilization.

therapies_index.name: vaginal delivery
approved_indications: A possible mode of delivery for a woman with Gaucher disease who has a hip prosthesis.
therapies_index.administration: Plan support from traumatology and rehabilitation when the woman has a hip prosthesis.

therapies_index.name: cesarean delivery
approved_indications: May be performed when needed despite hepatosplenomegaly; Gaucher disease alone does not make cesarean delivery necessary.
therapies_index.administration: If cesarean delivery is needed, a low transversal incision is recommended.

therapies_index.name: epidural anesthesia
therapies_index.administration: Contraindicated when platelet count is less than 70,000/mm3 or platelet function is impaired.
monitoring: Assess platelet count and platelet function.

therapies_index.name: breastfeeding
approved_indications: Recommended for mothers with Gaucher disease unless they have severe osteoporosis or uncontrolled disease; avoiding breastfeeding in those circumstances is suggested.
monitoring: Consider maternal osteoporosis severity and Gaucher disease control.

recognition: Bleeding can complicate pregnancy, delivery, or the postpartum period in women with GD, particularly when platelet function is impaired.
Platelet number and function are relevant to bleeding risk; platelet function testing is considered reliable when the platelet count exceeds 100,000 /mm3.

management.severity: Platelet count less than 70,000/mm3 or impaired platelet function

prevention: Assess platelet function during the third trimester.
When considering IVF, individualize the decision using platelet count, reliable platelet function results, and the risks of ovarian puncture bleeding and fetal loss.
Plan delivery in a hospital with immediate access to a blood bank and monitor for bleeding during delivery.

toxicities.event: Gestational thrombocytopenia or worsening thrombocytopenia in GD
toxicities.incidence: Gestational thrombocytopenia occurs in approximately between 5–11% of all pregnancies; by itself, it does not increase maternal bleeding risk.
recognition: Women with GD may have thrombocytopenia that worsens during pregnancy.
Impaired platelet function can add to bleeding risk.
prevention: Assess platelet function during the third trimester.
Use Aspirin after IVF only when platelet function is normal and thrombocytopenia is not significant.

toxicities.event: Bone crises and worsening bone disease during pregnancy or lactation
recognition: Pregnancy and lactation can increase skeletal calcium demand and potentially increase the risk of bone crises, osteopenia, osteonecrosis, and fractures.
Bone pain, bone crises, osteoporosis, and worsening bone pathology may occur in women with GD.

management.severity: Bone crisis or exacerbation of bone pathology during pregnancy
Severe osteoporosis or uncontrolled GD during lactation

prevention: Provide calcium and vitamin D supplements during pregnancy and breastfeeding.

toxicities.event: Anemia associated with low vitamin B12 during pregnancy
recognition: Pregnant women with GD have a particular risk of anemia and neuropathy related to vitamin B12 status.
Check vitamin B12 levels during the first trimester.

management.severity: Low vitamin B12 levels detected at pregnancy diagnosis, up to week 9
management.actions: Provide vitamin B12 at therapeutic doses.

prevention: Ensure the required daily vitamin B12 intake before and during pregnancy.

recognition: Pulmonary hypertension is described as very rare; its risk is largely confined to women with GD1 who have undergone splenectomy and patients with GD type 3 who have known lung disease.
Use cardiac ultrasound before a planned pregnancy to assess for pulmonary hypertension.

management.severity: Inconclusive cardiac ultrasound or a result borderline for pulmonary hypertension
management.actions: Consider right heart catheterization as the reference technique after weighing its invasive risks and benefits with the patient.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Vaccinate against pneumococcus, meningococcus, Haemophilus influenzae, and influenza before a planned pregnancy.
prophylaxis.target_population: Women with GD who have undergone splenectomy and are planning pregnancy

prophylaxis.recommendation: The CDC advises a primary COVID-19 vaccine series, followed by booster doses when eligible.
Add calcium and vitamin D during pregnancy.
Provide preventive vitamin B12 to ensure the required daily dose; use therapeutic doses if low levels are found at pregnancy diagnosis, up to week 9.
prophylaxis.target_population: Women with GD before and during pregnancy

prophylaxis.recommendation: Provide vitamin D and calcium supplements.

For women with GD who conceive through IVF, Aspirin can be used when platelet function is normal and thrombocytopenia is not significant. Weigh its risks against the intended improvement in reproductive outcomes and reduction of IVF-associated thrombosis risk.
prophylaxis.target_population: Pregnant women with GD following IVF who have normal platelet function and no significant thrombocytopenia

infection_management.prevention: Vaccinate women with GD who have undergone splenectomy before a planned pregnancy.
Vaccinate women with GD who have undergone splenectomy before a planned pregnancy.
Vaccinate women with GD who have undergone splenectomy before a planned pregnancy.
Vaccinate women with GD who have undergone splenectomy before a planned pregnancy.
The CDC advises all adults without a spleen to receive a primary vaccine series and booster doses when eligible.

infection_management.management: Monitor women with GD for infections during delivery because the guide identifies an increased risk.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with mild symptoms who are not receiving ERT and intend to become pregnant.
decision_rules: Begin ERT before conception.

recommended_regimens.name: ERT
recommended_regimens.summary: Initiate enzyme replacement before pregnancy at 60 units/kg every two weeks.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Asymptomatic women who are not receiving ERT and plan a pregnancy.
decision_rules: Perform a comprehensive GD assessment; do not initiate treatment before pregnancy if the patient remains asymptomatic.

not_recommended.name: ERT
not_recommended.reason: The panel advises against starting treatment before pregnancy in asymptomatic women after comprehensive GD assessment.

response_assessment.method: Comprehensive GD assessment, including bone densitometry and cardiac ultrasound to exclude PH.
response_assessment.interpretation: If cardiac ultrasound is inconclusive or borderline for PH, consider right heart catheterization after assessing its risks and benefits with the patient.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women receiving ERT who become pregnant.
decision_rules: Continue ERT without suspending or changing it solely because of pregnancy, including during the first trimester.
If GD worsens during pregnancy, adjust the enzyme replacement dose.

recommended_regimens.name: ERT
recommended_regimens.summary: Maintain treatment through pregnancy; adjust its dose if GD exacerbates.

not_recommended.name: ERT suspension or modification solely because of pregnancy
not_recommended.reason: The panel advises continuing ERT even in the first trimester.

response_assessment.method: Measure lysoGb1 and/or chitotriosidase, calcium, vitamin D and vitamin B12.
Measure lysoGb1 and/or chitotriosidase, calcium and vitamin D.

supportive_care: Provide calcium and vitamin D during pregnancy.
Ensure the required daily vitamin B12 intake before and during pregnancy; give therapeutic doses if low levels are detected at pregnancy diagnosis, up to week 9.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Pregnancy care requires an individualized program directed by an expert multidisciplinary team rather than standard pregnancy surveillance alone.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women taking Miglustat or Eliglustat who plan to become pregnant.
decision_rules: Discontinue Miglustat or Eliglustat at least 3 months before pregnancy and change to ERT before conception.

recommended_regimens.name: ERT
recommended_regimens.summary: Replace the existing substrate reduction treatment with enzyme replacement before pregnancy.

not_recommended.name: Miglustat
not_recommended.reason: Treatment must be stopped at least 3 months before pregnancy and replaced with ERT.

not_recommended.name: Eliglustat
not_recommended.reason: Treatment must be stopped at least 3 months before pregnancy and replaced with ERT.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women receiving bisphosphonates who intend to become pregnant.
decision_rules: Stop bisphosphonates at least 6 months before pregnancy.
For longlasting bisphosphonates, stop treatment earlier, before the intended effect has ended.

not_recommended.name: bisphosphonates
not_recommended.reason: The panel requires discontinuation at least 6 months before pregnancy, or earlier for longlasting bisphosphonates.

decision_rules: Arrange the specified vaccinations and cardiac ultrasound to exclude PH before pregnancy.

recommended_regimens.name: vaccination
recommended_regimens.summary: Vaccinate against pneumococcus, meningococcus, Haemophilus influenzae and influenza.

supportive_care: The cited CDC guidance advises a primary COVID-19 vaccine series and booster doses when eligible for adults without a spleen.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with GD and fertility problems considering assisted reproduction.
decision_rules: Assisted reproduction can be used and is compatible with ERT.
Individualize the decision according to GD status, platelet count and function, and the risks associated with ASA, fetal loss and bleeding during ovarian puncture.

recommended_regimens.name: assisted reproduction techniques
recommended_regimens.summary: Assisted reproduction is an option for fertility problems in women with GD, including those receiving ERT.

response_assessment.method: Assess platelet count and, when the count is greater than 100,000 /mm3, platelet function.
response_assessment.interpretation: The panel describes platelet function testing as reliable above this platelet-count threshold.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Use shared decision-making after weighing reproductive outcomes, thrombosis risk, fetal loss and bleeding during ovarian puncture.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with GD undergoing IVF whose spouse is a GD carrier, or Ashkenazi Jews undergoing IVF when the donor's status is unknown.
treatment_pathways.biomarker_condition: GD carrier status in the spouse, or unknown donor status in the specified IVF setting.
decision_rules: Offer pre-implantation genetic diagnosis when the spouse carries GD; the recommendation also applies to Ashkenazi Jews when donor status is unknown.
If a GD carrier is identified, investigate possible glucocerebrosidase pseudo-deficiencies.

recommended_regimens.name: pre-implantation genetic diagnosis
recommended_regimens.summary: Use genetic assessment of embryos in the specified IVF circumstances.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Because the balance of fetal-loss risk and ovarian-puncture bleeding is unknown, shared decision-making with the patient and family is mandatory; the panel also calls for planned outcome recording in an active GD pregnancy sub-registry.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with GD who conceived through IVF and are pregnant.
decision_rules: Aspirin can be given if platelet function is normal and thrombocytopenia is not significant.

recommended_regimens.name: Aspirin
recommended_regimens.summary: Aspirin may be used after IVF in a pregnant woman with GD when the stated platelet conditions are met.

response_assessment.interpretation: Use is conditional on normal platelet function and absence of significant thrombocytopenia.

decision_rules: Use care tailored to the individual patient under an expert multidisciplinary team; standard high-risk pregnancy care alone is insufficient.
Provide calcium and vitamin D, and ensure the required daily vitamin B12 intake.
If vitamin B12 is low when pregnancy is diagnosed, up to week 9, provide therapeutic doses.

recommended_regimens.name: vitamin B12
recommended_regimens.summary: Provide enough vitamin B12 to meet the required daily dose before and during pregnancy; use therapeutic doses when low levels are detected at pregnancy diagnosis.

response_assessment.method: Measure chitotriosidase and/or lysoGb1, calcium, vitamin D and vitamin B12.
response_assessment.interpretation: Low vitamin B12 detected at pregnancy diagnosis, up to week 9, calls for therapeutic supplementation.

response_assessment.method: Measure chitotriosidase and/or lysoGb1, calcium and vitamin D.
Assess platelet function; evaluate liver and spleen size by ultrasound if this has not already been done during pregnancy care.
response_assessment.interpretation: The last-trimester ultrasound is intended to document or exclude hepatosplenomegaly.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document identifies increased risks of anemia and neuropathy as reasons to ensure vitamin B12 intake.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Pregnant women with GD whose partner is a GD carrier, or who conceived through IVF with an unknown donor.
treatment_pathways.biomarker_condition: GD carrier status in the partner, or unknown donor status in IVF.
decision_rules: Offer prenatal genetic diagnosis under the specified circumstances.
Recommend preconception assessment of carrier status in couples to inform embryo assessment and decisions concerning mutation type and risk.

recommended_regimens.name: prenatal genetic diagnosis
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer prenatal testing when the partner is a carrier or an IVF donor's status is unknown.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Pregnant women with GD who develop bone crises or worsening bone pathology.
decision_rules: Perform magnetic resonance imaging when a bone crisis occurs or bone pathology worsens.

recommended_regimens.name: magnetic resonance imaging
recommended_regimens.summary: Investigate bone crises or worsening bone disease during pregnancy.

response_assessment.timepoint: during a bone crisis or exacerbation of bone pathology

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Pregnant women with GD approaching delivery, including women with a hip prosthesis or hepatosplenomegaly.
decision_rules: Plan delivery in a hospital with GD expertise and immediate access to a blood bank.
Do not recommend cesarean delivery solely because the patient has GD.
Vaginal delivery remains possible with a hip prosthesis if traumatology and rehabilitation support are planned.
Hepatosplenomegaly does not prevent a cesarean section when one is needed; use a low transversal incision in that circumstance.

recommended_regimens.name: vaginal delivery
recommended_regimens.summary: Vaginal delivery is possible for patients with a hip prosthesis when traumatology and rehabilitation support have been arranged.

alternative_regimens.name: cesarean section
alternative_regimens.summary: A cesarean section can be performed when necessary despite hepatosplenomegaly; a low transversal incision is recommended.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Use when cesarean delivery is otherwise necessary, not solely because of GD.

not_recommended.name: cesarean delivery solely because of GD
not_recommended.reason: The panel states that GD itself does not necessitate cesarean delivery.

response_assessment.method: Study platelet function and use ultrasound to document or exclude hepatosplenomegaly if these assessments have not already occurred during pregnancy care.

supportive_care: Ensure immediate access to a blood bank.
Monitor particularly for bleeding and infections during delivery.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The panel considers the risk of miscarriage uncertain because the available literature is inconclusive.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Pregnant women with GD being considered for epidural anesthesia.
decision_rules: Do not use epidural anesthesia if the platelet count is less than 70,000/mm3 or platelet function is impaired.

not_recommended.name: epidural anesthesia
not_recommended.reason: A platelet count less than 70,000/mm3 or impaired platelet function contraindicates it.

response_assessment.interpretation: Impaired platelet function is a contraindication to epidural anesthesia.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Newborns of mothers with GD, particularly when paternal carrier status is unknown.
decision_rules: If paternal carrier status is unknown, use an enzymatic dried drop test instead of genetic testing.
If clinical suspicion remains high despite a negative dried drop result, consider repeating that test or performing a genetic study.
Provide standard newborn care to a newborn without GD unless the mother experienced a complication during pregnancy.

recommended_regimens.name: enzymatic dried drop test
recommended_regimens.summary: Use neonatal enzymatic screening rather than routine genetic testing when the father's carrier status is unknown.

alternative_regimens.name: genetic study
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider genetic assessment if clinical suspicion remains high after a negative dried drop result.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Persistent high clinical suspicion despite a possible false-negative dried drop result.

not_recommended.name: routine newborn genetic testing for GD
not_recommended.reason: The panel advises that it is unnecessary when enzymatic dried drop screening can be offered.

response_assessment.interpretation: False-negative results can occur sporadically; high clinical suspicion warrants consideration of repeat testing or a genetic study.

supportive_care: Use standard newborn care unless the mother had a pregnancy complication.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Mothers with GD who are breastfeeding.
decision_rules: Recommend breastfeeding up to 6 months, except that avoidance is suggested if the mother has severe osteoporosis or uncontrolled GD.
Continue ERT at the same previous dose throughout breastfeeding.
Provide vitamin D and calcium supplements.

recommended_regimens.name: breastfeeding
recommended_regimens.summary: Recommend breastfeeding up to 6 months, subject to the stated maternal disease and bone-health exceptions.

recommended_regimens.name: ERT
recommended_regimens.summary: Maintain enzyme replacement at the dose used previously while breastfeeding.

not_recommended.name: bisphosphonates
not_recommended.reason: The panel advises that nursing mothers with GD cannot receive them.

not_recommended.name: Miglustat
not_recommended.reason: The panel advises that nursing mothers with GD cannot receive it.

not_recommended.name: Eliglustat
not_recommended.reason: The panel advises that nursing mothers with GD cannot receive it.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Avoiding breastfeeding is suggested, rather than required, for severe osteoporosis or uncontrolled maternal GD. The breastfeeding recommendation is marked Weak in Table 4; the separate recommendation to breastfeed up to 6 months is described as Strong Agreement in the narrative.

special_populations.population: Women with Gaucher disease planning pregnancy
special_populations.considerations: Preconception genetic counseling and a comprehensive assessment 3–6 months before a planned pregnancy are recommended. Assessment includes bone densitometry and cardiac ultrasound to exclude pulmonary hypertension. An inconclusive or borderline cardiac ultrasound may warrant discussion of right heart catheterization with the patient.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Bisphosphonates should be stopped at least 6 months before pregnancy, or earlier for longlasting bisphosphonates if their intended effect persists longer.

special_populations.population: Women with Gaucher disease receiving enzyme replacement therapy who become pregnant
special_populations.considerations: Pregnancy, including the first trimester, is not a reason to interrupt or alter existing enzyme replacement therapy.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Continue enzyme replacement therapy without changing the established treatment solely because of pregnancy.

special_populations.population: Women with Gaucher disease not receiving enzyme replacement therapy before pregnancy
special_populations.considerations: Treatment decisions differ according to symptoms after a comprehensive assessment.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Asymptomatic women should not begin treatment before pregnancy. Women with mild symptoms should start enzyme replacement therapy before pregnancy at 60 units/kg every two weeks.

special_populations.population: Women with Gaucher disease receiving substrate reduction therapy who plan pregnancy
special_populations.considerations: Existing treatment with Miglustat or Eliglustat must be changed before conception.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Discontinue Miglustat or Eliglustat at least 3 months before pregnancy and switch to enzyme replacement therapy before pregnancy.

special_populations.population: Splenectomized women with Gaucher disease planning pregnancy
special_populations.considerations: Cardiac ultrasound is required to exclude pulmonary hypertension. Vaccination against pneumococcus, meningococcus, Haemophilus influenzae and influenza is recommended; the document also cites primary COVID-19 vaccination and eligible booster doses for adults without a spleen.

special_populations.population: Women with Gaucher disease and moderate to severe pulmonary hypertension
special_populations.considerations: Pregnancy is discouraged in this group. The document describes pulmonary hypertension as rare, with risk largely confined to splenectomized women with GD1 or patients with GD type 3 and known lung disease. Anemia, thrombocytopenia, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly and osteoporosis alone are not reasons to discourage pregnancy.

special_populations.population: Women with Gaucher disease undergoing assisted reproduction
special_populations.considerations: Assisted reproduction can be used for fertility problems and is compatible with enzyme replacement therapy. Decisions should account for platelet count and function, bleeding associated with ovarian puncture, fetal loss and the risks of acetyl salicylic acid (ASA). During pregnancy after in vitro fertilization, Aspirin may be used conditional on normal platelet function and the absence of significant thrombocytopenia.

special_populations.population: Women with Gaucher disease whose partner is a carrier or whose reproductive donor is unknown
special_populations.considerations: Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis is recommended for in vitro fertilization when the spouse is a GD carrier, or when the donor is unknown in Ashkenazi Jews. Prenatal genetic diagnosis may be offered when the partner is a carrier or the donor is unknown in in vitro fertilization. Shared decision-making is required because the balance of fetal-loss and ovarian-puncture bleeding risks is unknown.

Usual high-risk pregnancy care alone is insufficient; an expert multidisciplinary team should tailor surveillance. The recommended checks include disease markers and nutritional measures during pregnancy, platelet-function assessment in the third trimester, and ultrasound assessment for hepatosplenomegaly in the last trimester. Calcium and vitamin D supplementation and preventive provision of vitamin B12 are recommended.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: If vitamin B12 is low when pregnancy is diagnosed, up to week 9, provide therapeutic doses. Adjust the enzyme replacement treatment dose if Gaucher disease worsens during pregnancy.

special_populations.population: Pregnant women with Gaucher disease and bone crises or worsening bone disease
special_populations.considerations: Magnetic resonance imaging is recommended when bone crises or exacerbations of bone pathology occur during pregnancy.

special_populations.population: Women with Gaucher disease during childbirth
special_populations.considerations: Delivery should occur in a hospital with Gaucher disease expertise and immediate blood-bank access. Gaucher disease alone does not require cesarean delivery, and hepatosplenomegaly does not preclude a necessary cesarean section; a low transversal incision is recommended if cesarean delivery is needed. Bleeding and infections warrant particular monitoring.

special_populations.population: Pregnant women with Gaucher disease and a hip prosthesis
special_populations.considerations: Vaginal delivery remains possible when support from traumatology and rehabilitation is planned.

special_populations.population: Pregnant women with Gaucher disease and impaired platelet function or low platelet counts
special_populations.considerations: A platelet count less than 70,000/mm3 or impaired platelet function contraindicates epidural anesthesia.

special_populations.population: Newborns of mothers with Gaucher disease
special_populations.considerations: When the father's carrier status is unknown, an enzymatic dried drop test is preferred over genetic testing. If clinical suspicion remains high despite a potentially false-negative result, the test may be repeated or genetic testing considered. Newborns without Gaucher disease need care beyond usual newborn care only when the mother experienced a pregnancy complication.

Breastfeeding is recommended for up to 6 months, although avoidance is suggested if the mother has severe osteoporosis or uncontrolled Gaucher disease. Vitamin D and calcium supplementation is recommended.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Maintain enzyme replacement therapy at its previous dose during breastfeeding. Do not treat nursing mothers with bisphosphonates, Miglustat or Eliglustat.

recommendations.statement: Offer preconception genetic counseling to every patient with Gaucher disease who plans to have children.
recommendations.context: Applies to both women and men.

recommendations.statement: Patients with GD and fertility problems may use assisted reproduction techniques.
recommendations.context: The panel advises an individualized assessment of GD status, platelet number and function, and the risks of acetyl salicylic acid (ASA), fetal loss and bleeding during ovarian puncture before a shared decision.
recommendations.rationale: Platelet abnormalities may affect in vitro fertilization (IVF); platelet function testing is reliable when the count is greater than 100,000 /mm3.

recommendations.statement: Assisted reproduction techniques may be used alongside enzyme replacement therapy (ERT).
Offer pre-implantation genetic diagnosis with IVF when the partner carries GD; it may also be offered to Ashkenazi Jews when the donor's GD status is unknown.
recommendations.context: Investigate possible pseudo-deficiencies of glucocerebrosidase when a carrier is identified. Shared decision-making with the patient and family, and planned recording of outcomes in an active GD pregnancy sub-registry, are required.
recommendations.rationale: The balance of fetal-loss and ovarian-puncture bleeding risks against benefits is unknown.

recommendations.statement: Discourage pregnancy when pulmonary hypertension is moderate to severe.
recommendations.context: The document describes this complication as very rare and its risk as largely restricted to splenectomized women with GD1 or patients with GD type 3 and known lung disease.

recommendations.statement: Do not regard anemia (Hb < 10 g/dl), thrombocytopenia (< 70,000 dl), hepatomegaly or splenomegaly (> 2 times normal), or osteoporosis alone as reasons to discourage pregnancy.
recommendations.context: Discuss potential risks and measures to address them, including calcium and vitamin D where needed.

recommendations.statement: Complete a comprehensive GD assessment 3–6 months before a planned pregnancy.
recommendations.context: In addition to routine GD monitoring, include bone densitometry and cardiac ultrasound to exclude pulmonary hypertension. If cardiac ultrasound is inconclusive or borderline for pulmonary hypertension, consider right heart catheterization after assessing risks and benefits and agreeing on the decision with the patient.
recommendations.rationale: Assessment before conception allows time to address GD-related problems; detecting pulmonary hypertension offers substantial potential benefit despite its rarity.

recommendations.statement: Stop bisphosphonates at least 6 months before pregnancy; stop longlasting bisphosphonates earlier, before their intended period of effect ends.
recommendations.context: Women receiving bisphosphonates who plan pregnancy.

recommendations.statement: Before a planned pregnancy, vaccinate women who have undergone splenectomy against pneumococcus, meningococcus, Haemophilus influenzae and influenza, and perform cardiac ultrasound to exclude pulmonary hypertension.
recommendations.context: The document also cites the Centers for disease control and prevention (CDC) recommendation that adults without a spleen receive a primary COVID-19 vaccine series and booster doses when eligible.

recommendations.statement: Do not stop or alter established ERT because of pregnancy, including during the first trimester.
recommendations.context: Patients already receiving ERT.

recommendations.statement: Do not initiate ERT before pregnancy in asymptomatic patients with GD who are not receiving it, following a comprehensive GD evaluation.
Start ERT before pregnancy in patients with GD who have mild symptoms and are not receiving it, at 60 units/kg every two weeks.
Discontinue Miglustat or Eliglustat at least 3 months before pregnancy and switch to ERT before conception.
recommendations.context: Patients receiving substrate reduction therapy (SRT).

recommendations.statement: Provide each pregnant patient with GD an individualized care program led by an expert multidisciplinary team rather than relying solely on standard high-risk pregnancy care.
recommendations.rationale: Standard high-risk pregnancy care is not sufficiently specific for GD.

recommendations.statement: During the first trimester, measure lysoGb1 and/or chitotriosidase, calcium, vitamin D and vitamin B12 levels.
recommendations.context: Pregnant patients with GD.

recommendations.statement: Aspirin may be used during pregnancy following IVF if platelet function is normal and thrombocytopenia is not significant.
recommendations.context: Pregnant patients with GD following IVF.

recommendations.statement: Provide calcium and vitamin D during pregnancy, and supply vitamin B12 preventively to meet the required daily dose before and during pregnancy; use therapeutic vitamin B12 doses if low levels are detected.
recommendations.context: Low vitamin B12 identified at pregnancy diagnosis, up to week 9, calls for therapeutic dosing.
recommendations.rationale: The document identifies a particular risk of anemia and neuropathy.

recommendations.statement: In the second and third trimesters, measure chitotriosidase and/or lysoGb1, calcium and vitamin D levels.
recommendations.context: Pregnant patients with GD.

recommendations.statement: Assess platelet function during the third trimester.
recommendations.context: Pregnant patients with GD.

recommendations.statement: Perform an ultrasound study in the last trimester to establish whether hepatosplenomegaly is present.
recommendations.context: The document particularly calls for liver and spleen size assessment if this has not been done earlier in pregnancy.
recommendations.rationale: The finding can inform planning if cesarean delivery becomes necessary.

recommendations.statement: Perform magnetic resonance imaging when bone crises or worsening bone pathology occur during pregnancy.
recommendations.context: Pregnant patients with GD.

recommendations.statement: Adjust the ERT dose if GD worsens during pregnancy.
Prenatal genetic diagnosis may be offered to a pregnant woman with GD if her partner carries GD or, following IVF, if the donor's status is unknown.
Perform a preconception genetic study of carrier status in couples.
recommendations.context: This informs identification of embryos carrying one GD mutation or two mutations and decisions based on mutation type and risk.

recommendations.statement: Plan delivery in a hospital with GD expertise and immediate access to a blood bank.
Do not recommend cesarean delivery solely because the patient has GD.
Vaginal delivery is possible for a patient with GD and a hip prosthesis when traumatology and rehabilitation support is planned.
Hepatosplenomegaly does not preclude a cesarean section when one is needed; use a low transversal incision.
Do not use epidural anesthesia if the platelet count is less than 70,000/mm3 or platelet function is impaired.
recommendations.context: Pregnant patients with GD.

recommendations.statement: Monitor particularly for bleeding and infections during delivery in women with GD.
recommendations.context: The panel identifies increased bleeding and postpartum infection risks.

recommendations.statement: Do not routinely perform genetic testing for GD in the newborn when enzymatic dried drop neonatal screening is available; use the enzymatic test if the father's carrier status is unknown.
recommendations.context: If clinical suspicion remains high despite a negative dried drop result, the test may be repeated or genetic testing considered.
recommendations.rationale: The dried drop test can sporadically yield false negatives.

recommendations.statement: Provide standard newborn care to a child without GD whose mother has GD, unless she experienced a complication during pregnancy.
recommendations.context: A maternal pregnancy complication may warrant different newborn follow-up.

recommendations.statement: Recommend breastfeeding for mothers with GD for up to 6 months.
recommendations.context: The separate recommendation to avoid breastfeeding in severe osteoporosis or uncontrolled GD has Weak Agreement; Table 4 assigns Weak to the combined breastfeeding recommendation.

recommendations.statement: Continue ERT during breastfeeding at the same dose used previously.
Give vitamin D and calcium supplements to breastfeeding mothers with GD.
Do not treat breastfeeding mothers with GD with bisphosphonates.
Do not treat breastfeeding mothers with GD with Miglustat or Eliglustat.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Gaucher disease may affect pregnancy, birth and lactation, with consequences for mothers and newborns; enzyme replacement therapy further complicates care. Evidence is inconclusive because appropriate clinical trials are unavailable. This guide aims to address clinical decisions before, during and after pregnancy and inform professionals, patients and families. Its authors used GRADE to assess evidence and formulate recommendations, followed by a structured 2-round Delphi consensus involving Gaucher experts. The abstract reports nine recommendations concerning preparation for pregnancy, genetic counseling and pregnancy care, seven concerning childbirth, and eight concerning care after delivery and breastfeeding. Patient values and preferences were considered alongside evidence quality. The authors propose that guidance combining available evidence and expert opinion may help patients and professionals who lack access to specialist Gaucher centers.

document_sections.heading: Background
document_sections.content: Gaucher disease (GD: MIM#230800) is an inherited metabolic condition caused by mutations in the gene encoding glucocerebrosidase (acid β-glucosidase; EC 3.2.1.45). Reduced β -glucocerebrosidase activity leads to glucosylceramide accumulation in monocyte-macrophage cells. Its non-neuropathic form, type 1, is the most common lysosomal storage disorder. Manifestations range from none to severe splenomegaly with hypersplenism, thrombocytopenia, anemia and leucopenia; hepatomegaly, coagulation abnormalities and bone disease may also occur. Bone manifestations include pain, crises, altered bone remodeling, osteopenia, osteonecrosis and pathological fractures; some patients have pulmonary involvement. Reproductive health in women with type 1 GD may be affected across fertility, pregnancy, delivery, the postpartum period and lactation. Information is limited and comes chiefly from case series. Multiorgan disease and coagulation abnormalities complicate pregnancy and birth. Hemoglobin declines during pregnancy, and gestational thrombocytopenia occurs in approximately between 5–11% of all pregnancies without increasing maternal bleeding risk. In GD, these changes may be more pronounced; impaired platelet function can contribute to excessive bleeding during pregnancy, birth or postpartum. Visceromegaly may impair fetal growth or affect delivery mode, as may GD-related orthopedic complications. Pregnancy and lactation place high calcium demands on the maternal skeleton and may increase the risk of bone crises, osteopenia, osteonecrosis and fractures. Pregnancy may worsen GD or reveal new manifestations. Its course varies mainly with disease severity and treatment control at conception. Hepatosplenomegaly, bone crises, osteoporosis and anemia can increase, thrombocytopenia can worsen, and symptoms appearing during pregnancy may prompt a first GD diagnosis. Specific GD treatments comprise enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) with velaglucerase alfa, imiglucerase or taliglucerase alfa, and substrate reduction therapy (SRT) with eliglustat or miglustat; not all are usable during pregnancy or lactation. Management before conception, during pregnancy and after delivery is challenging. Clinical trials are absent because of the patient numbers required and the ethical problems of placebo use. Previously published decision support consists of a few older consensus statements or expert opinions; guidance on in vitro fertilization and preimplantation genetic screening for women with GD is lacking. The article addresses genetic counseling; treatment across reproductive stages; childbirth and breastfeeding; prevention of maternal and child hematologic and bone complications; and information for patients and families.

document_sections.heading: Materials and methods
document_sections.content: The project followed the 2016 methodological manual for clinical practice guidelines of the Spanish National Health System and used Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) to assess evidence quality and recommendation strength. A survey explored the decisions and disease-specific concerns of clinicians and patients. The development group organized care into 4 stages: pre-pregnancy and genetic counseling, pregnancy, childbirth, and postpregnancy and breastfeeding. Questions covering distinct issues across these stages produced 56 PICO items.

document_sections.heading: Evidence search
document_sections.content: The authors sought studies published between January 2000 and April 2021 without restricting language or article type. The PubMed search combined ‘Gaucher disease’ with terms for pregnancy, fertility, childbirth, labor, genetic counseling, infant feeding, and maternal and child outcomes. Corresponding controlled vocabulary was used in Scopus, EBSCO, Academic Search Complete, CINAHL and Biomedical Reference. Because few publications were available, the search also covered grey literature, selected journals and conference proceedings, opinion articles, guidelines, consensus documents and their supporting references.

document_sections.heading: Studies selection
document_sections.content: Two reviewers, EJC and IML, examined the identified studies. Given the small number retrieved, they excluded only duplicate articles.

document_sections.heading: Data extraction
document_sections.content: EJC, IML and ARF independently classified studies by design and attempted to extract evidence on available standards of care for the four proposed clinical scenarios.

document_sections.heading: Consensus process
document_sections.content: The panel comprised nine experienced GD experts from 6 specialties—hematology, internal medicine, genetics, biochemistry, pediatrics and gynecology—and a midwife. Recommendations underwent a structured 2-round DelphiRAND process with anonymous ratings, controlled feedback and statistical aggregation. In round 1, panelists rated statements on a 9-point Likert scale; higher scores indicated greater agreement, and consensus was not forced. Round 2 sought to distinguish genuine clinical disagreement from fatigue or misunderstanding and resolve remaining discordance. IM analyzed the initial ratings; EC and AR reviewed the findings and revised statements with communication problems. The nine experts received a summary of round 1. Median scores of 7 or higher represented “strong” agreement (51.3%); scores of 4 to 6 represented “uncertain” agreement (27,6%); and scores of 1 to 3 represented “disagreement (21%). Statements with a median of 7 or higher but individual ratings from 1 to 6 were voted on again. Statements without agreement or disagreement were resubmitted with explanatory text. A brainstorming meeting with patient associations addressed patient values and preferences. EC, AR and IM drafted recommendations from the Delphi results. Panelists then accepted or rejected each revised recommendation by ‘yes / no’ vote. Minor language and structural edits were permitted without changing intent, and all panel members approved the final draft.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: Evidence concerning GD and pregnancy was scarce. The search yielded 36 references, classified as 3 prospective observational series comprising 64 pregnancies, 6 retrospective observational series comprising 505 pregnancies, 9 case records, and 8 narrative reviews and opinion article mainly concerning pre-pregnancy and genetic counseling. Reviewers agreed that evidence quality was low because publication dates, sample sizes, treatments and reported outcomes varied. The authors drafted 32 recommendations: 9 for preparation and genetic counseling, 9 for pregnancy, 7 for childbirth, and 7 for postpartum and breastfeeding. The panel did not agree on recommendations for fertility problems in GD, delayed menarche or the specific role of midwives. Agreement was strong for 24 recommendations, described as applicable to most patients in most circumstances, and weak for 8, for which circumstances or patient and societal values may make other options equally reasonable. Recommendations are organized by care stage, with agreement strength shown alongside them.

document_sections.heading: Panel recommendations Actions before pregnancy
document_sections.content: 1.1 Offer preconception genetic counseling to every patient with GD who wishes to have children (Strong Agreement). 1.2 Patients with GD and fertility difficulties may use assisted reproduction, including while receiving ERT (Strong Agreement). Because platelet number or function may affect in vitro fertilization (IVF), care should be individualized to GD status; platelet-function testing is reliable when the count is greater than 100,000 /mm3. Assess the risks of acetyl salicylic acid (ASA) use, thrombosis, fetal loss and bleeding from ovarian puncture, and make the assisted-reproduction decision jointly with the patient. 1.3 Offer pre-implantation genetic diagnosis in IVF if the partner carries GD or donor status is unknown (Weak Agreement). When carrier status is detected, investigate possible glucocerebrosidase pseudodeficiency. For Ashkenazi Jews, testing can also be undertaken when the partner’s GD status is unknown to assist detection of specific embryonic mutations. Because the balance of fetal-loss and ovarian-puncture bleeding risks is unknown, shared decision-making with the patient and family is mandatory, as is planned recording of outcomes in an active GD pregnancy sub-registry. 1.4 Pregnancy may be discouraged on health grounds, particularly with moderate to severe pulmonary hypertension (PH), which is very rare and whose risk is largely limited to splenectomized GD1 women or patients with GD type 3 and known lung disease (Strong Agreement). The panel identifies no eugenic grounds for discouragement. Anemia (Hb < 10 g/dl), thrombocytopenia (< 70,000 dl), hepatomegaly or splenomegaly (> 2 times normal), and osteoporosis do not themselves justify discouraging pregnancy. Discuss associated risks and possible measures, including calcium or vitamin D. Pregnancy may also be discouraged because of concurrent illnesses unrelated to GD, such as uncontrolled severe arterial hypertension, brittle diabetes mellitus, systemic lupus erythematosus or psychiatric problems. 1.5 Undertake a comprehensive GD assessment 3–6 months before a planned pregnancy (Strong Agreement). Alongside routine GD monitoring, include bone densitometry and cardiac ultrasound to exclude PH. If cardiac ultrasound is inconclusive or borderline for PH, right heart catheterization is the reference technique; weigh its invasive risks and benefits and decide with the patient. 1.6 Stop bisphosphonates at least 6 months before pregnancy, or earlier for long-lasting agents so that cessation precedes the end of their intended effect (Strong Agreement). 1.7 Before a planned pregnancy, splenectomized patients should receive vaccination against pneumococcus, meningococcus, Haemophilus influenzae and influenza, and undergo cardiac ultrasound to exclude PH (Strong Agreement). The cited Centers for disease control and prevention (CDC) also advise adults without a spleen to receive a primary COVID-19 vaccine series and eligible boosters. 1.8 Patients already receiving ERT should neither stop nor change it because of pregnancy, including in the first trimester. After comprehensive evaluation, asymptomatic patients not receiving ERT should not begin it before pregnancy; those with mild symptoms who are untreated should start ERT before pregnancy at 60 units/kg every two weeks (Strong Agreement). 1.9 Patients receiving Miglustat or Eliglustat should discontinue it at least 3 months before pregnancy and change to ERT before conception (Strong Agreement).

document_sections.heading: Gaucher disease management during pregnancy
document_sections.content: 2.1 Standard high-risk pregnancy care alone is insufficient; each pregnant patient with GD requires an individualized program led by an expert multidisciplinary team (Strong Agreement). 2.2 In the first trimester, measure lysoGb1 and/or chitotriosidase and/or, calcium, vitamin D and vitamin B12 levels (Strong Agreement). 2.3 Patients who conceive through IVF may receive Aspirin if platelet function is normal and thrombocytopenia does not preclude its use (Weak Agreement). 2.4 Provide calcium and vitamin D during pregnancy and preventive vitamin B12 sufficient to meet daily requirements before and during pregnancy because of particular anemia and neuropathy risks. If low B12 is found at pregnancy diagnosis, up to week 9, provide therapeutic doses (Strong Agreement). 2.5 During the second and third trimesters, measure lysoGb1 and/or chitotriosidase and/or lysoGb1, calcium and vitamin D levels (Strong Agreement). 2.6 In the third trimester, assess platelet function and, if not previously assessed during pregnancy, examine liver and spleen size by ultrasound (Strong Agreement). Available in vitro approaches to primary-hemostasis assessment include platelet function analyzer (PFA)100/200, platelet aggregometry, flow cytometry, and cone and platelet analyzer. PFA-100/200 is widely used for platelet-function assessment and has been proposed in place of ‘skin bleeding time’ to assess presurgical bleeding risk, but has not been tested in GD. In the sole cited GD study using the cone platelet (let) analyzer, reduced platelet adhesion was associated with mucosal bleeding whereas an aggregation defect was not. Neither method has specific evidence in pregnant women with GD. A last-trimester ultrasound is also recommended to establish whether hepatosplenomegaly is present, particularly when cesarean delivery is contemplated (Weak Agreement); a low transversal incision is recommended if cesarean delivery occurs. 2.7 Perform magnetic resonance imaging for bone crises or worsening bone disease during pregnancy (Strong Agreement). 2.8 Adjust the ERT dose when GD worsens during pregnancy (Strong Agreement). 2.9 Offer prenatal genetic diagnosis when the partner carries GD or, for IVF, the donor’s status is unknown (Weak Agreement). Preconception assessment of carrier status in couples is recommended to distinguish embryos carrying one GD mutation from those carrying two and affected by GD, and to inform decisions according to mutation type and risk.

document_sections.heading: Gaucher disease care during childbirth
document_sections.content: 3.1 Delivery should occur in a hospital experienced with GD and able to anticipate complications, including immediate access to a blood bank (Strong Agreement). 3.2 GD alone does not warrant cesarean delivery (Strong Agreement). 3.3 Vaginal birth remains possible with a hip prosthesis when traumatology and rehabilitation support is planned (Weak Agreement). 3.4 Hepatosplenomegaly does not prevent a necessary cesarean; use a low transversal incision (Strong Agreement). 3.5 A platelet count less than 70,000/mm3 or impaired platelet function contraindicates epidural anesthesia (Strong Agreement). 3.6 Whether miscarriage risk is higher in pregnant women with GD is uncertain: published findings are biased and inconsistent, and comparison with pregnant women without GD requires further research.

document_sections.heading: Table 1 Recommendations to prepare for pregnancy
document_sections.content: The table presents recommendations for preparation for pregnancy and their Strong or Weak strength. It covers genetic counseling for women and men, assisted reproduction, circumstances for pre-implantation diagnosis, moderate-severe pulmonary hypertension, assessment before conception, cessation of bisphosphonates, vaccination after splenectomy, and changes to GD-specific treatment.

document_sections.heading: Gaucher disease care during childbirth
document_sections.content: 3.7 The panel considers pregnant women with GD at increased risk of bleeding and postpartum infection (Strong Agreement).

document_sections.heading: Postpartum care
document_sections.content: 4.1 Routine genetic testing of the newborn is not recommended (Strong Agreement). If paternal GD carrier status is unknown, use an enzymatic dried drop neonatal screening test instead. False negatives occasionally occur; with strong clinical suspicion, the test could be repeated or genetic testing considered. 4.2 A newborn without GD whose mother has GD requires care beyond standard newborn care only if the mother experienced a pregnancy complication (Weak Agreement). 4.3 Recommend breastfeeding for up to 6 months (Strong Agreement), although avoiding it is suggested if maternal osteoporosis is severe or GD remains uncontrolled (Weak Agreement). 4.4 Continue ERT throughout breastfeeding at the previous dose (Strong Agreement). 4.5 Provide breastfeeding mothers with GD vitamin D and calcium supplements (Strong Agreement). 4.6 Do not treat breastfeeding mothers with bisphosphonates (Strong Agreement). 4.7 Do not treat breastfeeding mothers with Miglustat or Eliglustat (Strong Agreement). The recommendation strengths are summarized in Tables 1, 2, 3 and 4.

document_sections.heading: Clinical questions not addressed in the consensus process and that require further research
document_sections.content: Unresolved questions concern whether women and men with GD have more fertility problems than unaffected people, whether menarche is delayed in GD, and what specific role midwives should have in childbirth care for patients with GD.

document_sections.heading: Table 2 Recommendations during pregnancy
document_sections.content: The table summarizes pregnancy-care recommendations and their Strong or Weak strength. Its topics are individualized specialist care, trimester-specific laboratory checks, conditional Aspirin use after IVF, supplementation, platelet-function testing, ultrasound for hepatosplenomegaly, imaging for bone symptoms, treatment adjustment when GD worsens, and prenatal genetic diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: Table 3 Recommendations during childbirth
document_sections.content: The table summarizes childbirth recommendations with their Strong or Weak strength. It addresses delivery in a hospital with immediate blood-bank access, the absence of a routine cesarean indication, vaginal birth with a hip prosthesis, cesarean technique when hepatosplenomegaly is present, contraindications to epidural anesthesia, and particular monitoring for bleeding and infection during delivery.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: Women with type 1 Gaucher disease are often diagnosed shortly before or during reproductive age, and disease-related changes can affect fertility, pregnancy and childbirth. Effective treatments for type 1 GD exist, but guidance specific to their use during pregnancy has been lacking. Using a rigorous, reproducible approach, the authors developed 32 recommendations to support physicians caring for women with type 1 GD who are planning pregnancy or are pregnant. Recommendations are grouped around decisions before conception, during pregnancy, around delivery and during lactation. The authors expect guidance combining available evidence with expert opinion to assist patients, nurses, midwives and physicians with limited GD experience.

document_sections.heading: Table 4 Recommendations after delivery
document_sections.content: The table presents postpartum and breastfeeding recommendations with their Strong or Weak strength. It covers neonatal enzymatic screening and possible follow-up testing, newborn care according to maternal pregnancy complications, breastfeeding and maternal disease status, continuation of ERT, vitamin D and calcium supplementation, and avoidance of bisphosphonates, Miglustat and Eliglustat while nursing.
